faq.q1: How do I use this budget calculator?
faq.a1: Enter your net monthly income in the first section, then your fixed expenses (rent, insurance, etc.) and variable expenses (groceries, leisure, etc.). The calculator will automatically display your monthly balance.
faq.q2: What is the difference between fixed and variable expenses?
faq.a2: Fixed expenses are recurring amounts that don't change from month to month (rent, insurance, subscriptions). Variable expenses fluctuate based on your habits (groceries, gas, outings).
faq.q3: How do I export my budget to Excel?
faq.a3: Click the 'Export Excel' button to download a file containing three sheets: Summary, Details, and Category Distribution.

schlAlert.title: Mortgage Insurance Required (CMHC)
schlAlert.message: Your down payment is less than 20%. Insurance of {{amount}} will be added to your mortgage.

faq.a1: Mortgage loan insurance is required in Canada if your down payment is less than 20%. It protects the lender in case of default.
faq.q2: What is the minimum down payment to buy a house?
faq.a2: In Canada, the minimum down payment is 5% for properties up to $500,000. Between $500,000 and $1 million, it's 5% on the first $500,000 and 10% on the rest.
faq.q3: What is the difference between fixed and variable rates?
faq.a3: A fixed rate stays constant during the entire term. A variable rate fluctuates with the Bank of Canada's key rate.
faq.a4: Amortization is the total time planned to repay the mortgage. The maximum is 25 years with CMHC insurance, or 30 years without.
faq.q5: How can I reduce my mortgage payments?
faq.a5: You can increase your down payment, choose a longer amortization, shop rates between lenders, or opt for accelerated payments.

compound.explanation: Compound interest is often called 'the eighth wonder of the world.' It's the process by which your interest earns interest, creating a snowball effect on your investments over time.

faq.a1: Compound interest works by automatically reinvesting your earnings. Each period, interest is calculated on the initial capital plus all previously accumulated interest.
faq.q2: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
faq.a2: Simple interest is calculated only on the initial capital, while compound interest is calculated on the capital plus already accumulated interest.
faq.q3: How often should interest be compounded?
faq.a3: The higher the compounding frequency, the greater your gains. Monthly compounding generates more returns than annual compounding.
faq.q4: Why is starting to invest early so important?
faq.a4: Time is the most powerful factor of compound interest. Someone who invests early can accumulate more than someone who invests longer but starts late.
faq.a5: Historically, the Canadian stock market has generated about 7-8% per year long-term. A savings account offers 2-4%, a balanced portfolio 5-6%.

rrsp.explanation: The Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) is a tax-sheltered savings account designed to help you save for retirement. Contributions to your RRSP are deductible from your taxable income.
rrsp.workingExplanation: While still working, you can take more risks when investing because your salary can offset losses.
rrsp.retirementExplanation: Once retired, you can take fewer risks when investing because your salary can no longer offset losses.

faq.q1: What is the RRSP contribution limit for 2026?
faq.a1: For 2026, the RRSP contribution limit is 18% of your previous year's earned income, up to a maximum of $32,490.
faq.q2: When should I contribute to my RRSP?
faq.a2: You can contribute to your RRSP throughout the year and up to the 60th day of the following year for the contribution to be deductible.
faq.q3: RRSP or TFSA: which one to choose?
faq.a3: RRSP is generally preferable if your current tax rate is higher than in retirement. TFSA is advantageous if you expect a similar or higher rate.
faq.q4: Can I withdraw from my RRSP before retirement?
faq.a4: Yes, but withdrawals are taxable. Two exceptions: HBP (up to $60,000 for first home) and LLP (up to $20,000 for studies).
faq.q5: What happens to my RRSP at 71?
faq.a5: At the end of the year you turn 71, you must convert your RRSP to a RRIF, buy an annuity, or withdraw the balance.

fhsa.explanation: The First Home Savings Account (FHSA) is a new registered plan that combines the benefits of the RRSP and TFSA. It allows you to save up to $40,000 tax-free for your first home purchase.
fhsa.eligibilityIntro: Check your eligibility to open a First Home Savings Account (FHSA).
fhsa.firstTimeQuestion: Are you a first-time home buyer?

fhsa.notEligible: Based on your answers, you don't appear to be eligible for the FHSA.
fhsa.savingsIntro: Tell us how you're saving and we'll help calculate your potential savings.
fhsa.purchaseDate: When do you plan to buy your home?

faq.q1: What is the annual contribution limit for the FHSA?
faq.a1: The annual contribution limit for the FHSA is $8,000.
faq.q2: Can I have an FHSA if I owned a home 5 years ago?
faq.a2: Yes! You're eligible if you haven't owned a home in the preceding four calendar years.
faq.q3: What happens if I don't buy a home?
faq.a3: You have 15 years to use the funds. After that, you can transfer them to your RRSP or withdraw them taxably.
faq.q4: Can I combine the FHSA with the HBP?
faq.a4: Yes! You can use both for your down payment (up to $100,000 combined).
faq.q5: Is the FHSA better than the RRSP for buying a home?
faq.a5: For first home purchase, the FHSA is generally more advantageous because withdrawals are tax-free.

seo.keywords: net worth, assets, liabilities, wealth, calculator, personal finance

netWorth.explanation: Your net worth represents your real wealth: the difference between everything you own (assets) and everything you owe (liabilities). It's the best indicator of your overall financial health.

faq.a1: Net worth is the difference between what you own (assets) and what you owe (liabilities).
faq.q2: What should my net worth be for my age?
faq.a2: A general rule suggests your net worth should equal your age multiplied by your annual gross income, divided by 10.
faq.q3: Should I include my primary residence in my assets?
faq.a3: Yes, use its estimated market value. Don't forget to subtract your mortgage balance from your liabilities.
faq.q4: How can I increase my net worth?
faq.a4: Increase your assets (savings, investments) and reduce your liabilities (debt repayment).
faq.q5: How often should I calculate my net worth?
faq.a5: Calculate your net worth at least once a year, ideally at the same time each year.

debtConsolidation.consolidationExplanation: Debt consolidation is a strategy that involves combining multiple debts into a single loan.

faq.a1: Debt consolidation involves combining multiple debts into a single loan with a generally lower interest rate.
faq.q2: When should I consider debt consolidation?
faq.a2: Consider consolidation if you have multiple high-interest debts or have trouble keeping up with multiple payments.
faq.q3: What are the consolidation options in Canada?
faq.a3: Options include: a bank consolidation loan, a home equity line of credit, a credit card balance transfer.
faq.q4: Does consolidation affect my credit score?
faq.a4: Short-term, a loan application may slightly lower your score. Long-term, it can improve it.
faq.q5: What's the difference between consolidation and bankruptcy?
faq.a5: Consolidation is an agreement to repay your debts. Bankruptcy is a legal procedure with severe impact on your credit.

faq.q1: What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rates?
faq.a1: The marginal rate is the tax percentage on your next dollar. The effective rate is the total percentage on all your income.
faq.q2: How can I reduce my taxes?
faq.a2: Main strategies include: contributing to your RRSP or FHSA, maximizing tax credits, income splitting.
faq.q3: When do I need to file my tax return?
faq.a3: The deadline is generally April 30 for individuals and June 15 for self-employed.
faq.q4: Do I pay provincial and federal tax?
faq.a4: Yes, in Canada you pay both. Quebec collects its own provincial tax (two returns to file).
faq.a5: Quebec residents receive a 16.5% abatement on their federal tax because Quebec administers its own social programs.
